newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scientists say mines give good radon data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scientists say mines give good radon data.

text.p: Looking to see if the scare over cancer from radon was justified, scientists found that models based on studies of miners were a reasonable predictor of cancer risk from radon in homes.

But in an article to be published on Wednesday in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute they said more research should be completed for an accurate assessment of the cancer risk directly from indoor radon.

Fear of radon in houses was sparked many decades ago by studies which found that miners exposed to radon had a higher risk of dying from lung cancer. However, research in the last 10 years yielded mixed results on whether radioactive decay of radon indoors was a health hazard.

In an analysis of eight existing studies on lung cancer and radon in homes, two scientists concluded that despite differences between the studies involving a total of 4,263 lung cancer cases and 6,612 control subjects, it was fair to extrapolate lung cancer risks in homes based on miner studies.

Jay Lubin of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda, Maryland, and partner John Boice, Jr. of the International Epidemiology Institute in Rockville, Maryland, summarized the eight studies, adjusting for differences such as the age of the participants and the duration of the different studies.
"Overall there was a deleterious effect with long-term residence in higher radon houses, which was very consistent with miner-based studies," Lubin said in a telephone interview.

The scientists also said the small increase in cancer risk due to radon found in home studies was in line with miner studies. They concluded that "the risk from indoor radon is not likely to be markedly greater than that predicted from miners."

Lubin said summarizing published studies had drawbacks compared with pooling actual data, because many factors could not be controlled, such as the number of subjects who were smokers and the duration of exposure.
Eleven studies on homes are in the works and data from existing studies are going to be pooled with them.
